title: DELETE
description: Remove exactly the intended row population while retaining its table contract, preserve the salary-threshold checker, and distinguish predicate correctness from dependency, transaction and recovery guarantees.
notes:
## Deletion removes rows while preserving a usable definition

DELETE removes selected rows from an existing table. The table's columns and relevant definition remain for permitted later operations. A campus cleanup can remove expired staging records without removing the staging table itself. This is different from DROP TABLE, which removes the object, and from an UPDATE that merely changes a status value on the existing row.

The retained exercise removes employees whose salary is less than 60000. It is a synthetic predicate lesson, not a real employment policy. The important SQL contract is that selected identities disappear while every nonmatching supplied employee remains. A solution must not replace the whole table with a memorized list of survivors or infer a different cutoff from the sample.

## WHERE defines membership in the removal set

A condition such as salary < 60000 excludes a salary exactly at 60000. Replacing < with <= would remove that boundary row and answer a different question. A missing predicate in an ordinary unrestricted DELETE can make all rows eligible, subject to actual execution settings, permissions and applicable integrity rules.

For the introductory cleanup, both expired=1 and state=staging must hold. An expired published row stays, and a nonexpired staging row stays. These candidates are useful because each satisfies only one half of the conjunction. Testing them exposes a mistaken OR or omitted condition that might otherwise look correct on an all-matching sample.

```sql
DELETE FROM employees
WHERE salary < 60000;
```

## Preserve every nonmatching fact deliberately

The expected result after deletion includes the survivors, not only a count of removed rows. A count alone can hide removal of the wrong identities when another equally sized population remains. The retained checker reads id and name in identifier order so the assessment can observe precisely which supplied employees survived.

Names are descriptions rather than reliable identity. If two employees share a name but only one has a below-threshold salary, the predicate should still operate on each row's accepted values. Do not use name-only deduplication to manufacture a survivor set. The target's primary key keeps the identity distinction explicit while the removal condition addresses the stated salary property.

## NULL predicates need the same careful logic as reads

A WHERE condition must be TRUE for the row to qualify. An ordinary comparison with NULL can be UNKNOWN, which does not select the row. A task that wants to remove missing values should use the appropriate IS NULL predicate rather than equality to a displayed missing marker. The retained salary table requires salary, so that absence policy is outside its positive fixture domain.

Absence-based deletes using NOT IN can also be affected by NULL in the compared source. A correctly scoped NOT EXISTS can express a missing relationship under its own assumptions. Do not swap these forms mechanically while assuming every missing-value case stays equivalent. The simple tasks avoid that complexity, but their explanation should not promote an unsafe universal anti-join shortcut.

## Reference rules can reject or extend an accepted delete

A parent row can have dependent child references. Under an enforced restrictive reference, removing that parent can be rejected. A supported CASCADE action can remove associated children, while SET NULL has its own requirements. Those outcomes follow the actual declared rule, not a generic promise that every DELETE affects only the base table named in its text.

Other configured triggers can also contribute effects. Inspect the relevant definitions before predicting the final accepted state. A temporary-table cleanup with no such dependencies cannot prove native persistent referential actions, and a successful synthetic employee removal does not authorize deleting an authoritative parent from the application's shared database. Object, actor and rule scope remain important.

## Transaction support belongs to the actual storage contract

A DELETE on transactional InnoDB data participates in supported transaction behaviour. Before successful commit, an appropriate rollback can restore its transactional row changes under that contract. Nontransactional engines, surrounding DDL and additional effects can differ. It is inaccurate to say every DELETE in every possible environment is fully reversible merely because the verb is DML.

A client also needs correct error and completion handling. A failed statement is not automatically proof that all earlier workflow steps or external actions were undone. The exercises verify isolated post-delete rows and do not contact other systems. A real multi-step removal process needs a deliberate transaction boundary and recovery policy matching the full operation.

## Previewing helps review the intended candidate set

A SELECT with the proposed predicate can reveal which rows satisfy a cleanup condition. Include the relevant identity and condition roles in that preview, especially for compound filters or exact cutoffs. This makes it easier to see that an expired published row is outside the requested staging-only cleanup or that salary 60000 must remain.

The preview is still an observation at its own time and isolation context. Concurrent changes can make a later write see a different population unless the workflow coordinates them appropriately. A preview also does not grant permission to remove the rows. It is useful correctness evidence within the preparation process, not an automatic authorization or concurrency guarantee.

## Whole-table removal is not a universal truncate replacement

DELETE without a filter and TRUNCATE can both leave a table without old rows, but their transaction, trigger, dependency and identity-state behaviour can differ. MySQL truncation has its own DDL and counter-reset semantics, while ordinary deletion does not imply the same reset. Compare the required postcondition rather than assume one is merely a faster interchangeable spelling.

Performance also depends on the engine and workload. A table-level reset can avoid a particular row-delete path, but claims of no logging or guaranteed instant completion are too broad. If a subset must remain, truncation is already the wrong logical operation regardless of speed. Measure relevant alternatives only after they preserve the actual accepted-data contract.

## Archival and deletion need explicit coordination

A workflow may copy rows to an archive before removing the originals. That is two state changes, not an automatic feature of DELETE. A supported transaction can coordinate their atomic acceptance, while the selected identity set and concurrency policy still need to ensure the copy and removal concern the intended same facts.

A backup is also not an immediate undo button for an arbitrary deletion. Its coverage, freshness and restoration procedure determine what can be recovered. These notes explain the boundary without executing production archival or promising an untested recovery. The retained exercise removes only supplied disposable rows and expects no invented replacement or hidden archive side effect.

## Repeating a delete differs from proving an idempotent workflow

Once a specific qualifying row is gone, an immediate repeat over unchanged input cannot remove that same stored occurrence again. That narrow observation does not make a broader cleanup automatically idempotent. New qualifying rows, changing predicates, triggers or downstream actions can alter the repeated operation's meaning.

A production retry design needs to know the accepted removal set and which additional effects are tied to the request. Do not infer complete once-only behaviour from the fact that a second SELECT returns fewer rows. The exercises remain controlled state transitions with fixed synthetic inputs, so their expected result does not require speculative claims about every later retry or job schedule.

## Preserve the original post-write checker

The low-salary task's original checker selects id and name from employees after the student's DELETE. The reference submission therefore contains the write only, leaving the checker to produce its expected result set. Original schema, sample rows, checker and problem identity are retained so previous assessment semantics are not silently changed by the content rebuild.

Hidden fixtures vary the salaries and identities while preserving the same strict cutoff. Additional cases include salary exactly 60000, one just below it and an empty table. Those cases distinguish < from <=, verify survivor preservation and ensure the solution does not invent rows. The task does not ask to modify salary or reinterpret department membership.

## Test every side of the cleanup condition

The introductory task includes expired staging, expired published and current staging records. Only the first is removed. A fixture with several qualifying ids verifies the predicate applies to all requested candidates rather than only the first match. A fixture with no candidates leaves every supplied row intact, while empty input remains empty.

These checks establish a useful deletion contract without relying on an affected-row count whose provider interpretation may need separate review. Read the final identities and fields to verify what remains. Where real dependencies or triggers exist, their additional effects need their own relevant assertions rather than assume these simple temporary fixtures cover them.

## Keep completion claims tied to the actual environment

A useful illustration follows predicate truth to removed or preserved identity. The notes, MCQs and expected outputs should agree on exact boundaries, conjunctions and retained table structure. That makes DELETE understandable as a specific accepted-state transition rather than a command whose correctness follows from returning a success acknowledgment.

Recorded MariaDB compatibility fixtures verify the supplied cleanup and retained salary-removal cases. Exact MySQL/provider execution, untested native dependencies, production concurrency and recovery remain separate checks. The prepared content migration stores instructional definitions only; it does not remove application employees or deploy a cleanup process. A complete learning package can accurately explain deletion while leaving those unperformed operational claims open.

questions.question_text: What does DELETE do?
options: Removes rows matching a condition, leaving the table structure intact
questions.explanation: DELETE removes rows only; the table itself (columns, indexes, constraints) remains.

questions.question_text: Under an enforced restrictive parent reference, what can a DELETE of the referenced parent do?
options: The delete succeeds and the child row's reference becomes invalid
Be rejected to preserve the accepted reference
The child row is automatically deleted too
The parent row's key is automatically changed
questions.explanation: Other declared actions and timing modes have their own outcomes.

questions.question_text: Why can whole-table TRUNCATE have different cost from DELETE?
options: TRUNCATE and DELETE have identical performance in every engine
The engine can use a different table-level path with different semantics
DELETE always fails on large tables
TRUNCATE only works on empty tables
questions.explanation: This does not mean zero logging or universal speed, and it cannot preserve a WHERE subset.

questions.question_text: When is rollback of deleted rows a supported expectation?
options: No, DELETE is always immediately permanent
Within the actual transactional engine and uncommitted operation contract
Only if no WHERE clause is used
questions.explanation: Do not generalize to nontransactional engines or every surrounding side effect.

questions.question_text: What is the safety practice recommended before running a DELETE with an uncertain WHERE clause?
options: Run it directly and check the result afterward
Preview the affected rows first with an equivalent SELECT using the same WHERE clause
Always delete without a WHERE clause to be thorough
questions.explanation: Previewing with SELECT is the standard, reliable safety practice.

questions.question_text: Does DELETE change a table's column structure?
options: No — DELETE only removes rows; columns, indexes, and constraints remain unchanged
DELETE always resets the table's AUTO_INCREMENT counter
questions.explanation: DELETE is purely a row-removal operation with no effect on the table's structure.

questions.question_text: Can DELETE be filtered to remove only specific rows?
options: No, DELETE always removes every row
Yes — a WHERE clause targets DELETE to only the matching rows
DELETE can only remove exactly one row at a time
questions.explanation: WHERE is exactly what makes DELETE selective rather than total.

questions.question_text: What must a DELETE-versus-TRUNCATE choice compare?
options: No trade-off — TRUNCATE is strictly better in every way
Required population, structure, identity, triggers, dependencies and transaction rules before measured cost
DELETE is always faster than TRUNCATE
TRUNCATE always requires a WHERE clause, unlike DELETE
questions.explanation: A vague faster-or-safer slogan is not a complete semantic comparison.

questions.question_text: Does salary exactly 60000 match salary<60000?
questions.explanation: The cutoff is strict.

questions.question_text: Which cleanup row matches expired=1 AND state=staging?
questions.explanation: Both conditions are required.

questions.question_text: Does DELETE remove the table definition?
questions.explanation: Row removal differs from DROP.

questions.question_text: Why read survivor identities rather than only a removed count?
options: An equal count could hide removal of the wrong rows
questions.explanation: The postcondition includes which facts remain.

questions.question_text: Does a separate preview guarantee an unchanged concurrent population?
questions.explanation: Observation and coordinated mutation are different boundaries.

questions.question_text: Can declared cascades extend effects beyond the named base table?
questions.explanation: Actual reference rules determine the accepted outcome.

questions.question_text: Does ordinary deletion imply MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT reset?
options: Only when all rows are gone
questions.explanation: The generator’s state differs from row population.

questions.question_text: Is archive creation automatic in DELETE?
questions.explanation: Copying and removal require an explicit workflow.

questions.question_text: Why must a missing-value cleanup use the appropriate predicate?
options: Ordinary equality with NULL is not TRUE for the missing marker
Every absent value is empty text
questions.explanation: SQL truth semantics determine selection.

questions.question_text: What should the retained salary-removal submission produce directly?
options: Only the write; the original checker supplies the read
questions.explanation: Preserve the assessment’s execution contract.

questions.question_text: Does a second unchanged delete prove once-only downstream effects universally?
questions.explanation: A broader retry workflow needs its own policy.

questions.question_text: What remains outside the fixture evidence?
options: Production recovery and exact provider behaviour
questions.explanation: The actual tested scope is narrower than live operation readiness.

coding_problems.title: Remove only expired staging records
coding_problems.task: Delete records where expired=1 AND state=staging. Preserve expired published rows and current staging rows. Return record_id,state,expired for every survivor. Do not drop or replace the supplied table.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE records (record_id INT PRIMARY KEY,state VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,expired INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Retain the table definition and all nonmatching facts.
edge_cases: Only one predicate match is insufficient.
hints: Use the conjunction rather than OR.
Read the complete surviving population afterward.
coding_problems.solution_sql: DELETE FROM records WHERE expired=1 AND state='staging'; SELECT record_id,state,expired FROM records ORDER BY record_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The predicate isolates the exact disposable population and preserves every supplied nonmatching record.

coding_problems.title: Remove Low-Salary Employees
coding_problems.original_check_sql: SELECT id, name FROM employees ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.check_sql: SELECT id, name FROM employees ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.task: Delete every supplied employee with salary<60000. Preserve employees at the exact boundary and above it. This synthetic exercise teaches the strict predicate, not employment policy. Submit the write only; the original checker reads surviving id,name rows in id order.
coding_problems.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO employees (id, name, department, salary) VALUES

constraints: Original identity, schema, sample rows and checker retained.
No unrelated department filter or salary update.
hints: The checker reads only after your deletion.
coding_problems.explanation: The strict cutoff removes the requested synthetic subset while preserving the original checker and every nonmatching identity.

original_questions.question_text: What happens if a DELETE targets a row still referenced by a child table's foreign key, with no cascading action configured?
options: The delete succeeds and the child row's reference becomes invalid
The delete is rejected, preventing an orphaned reference
The child row is automatically deleted too
The parent row's key is automatically changed
original_questions.explanation: Referential integrity blocks a delete that would orphan existing child references, absent a cascading action.

original_questions.question_text: Why is TRUNCATE typically faster than DELETE FROM table with no WHERE, for emptying an entire table?
options: TRUNCATE and DELETE have identical performance in every engine
TRUNCATE deallocates the whole data structure at once rather than removing rows one by one with full transaction logging
DELETE always fails on large tables
TRUNCATE only works on empty tables
original_questions.explanation: TRUNCATE's bulk deallocation approach avoids the per-row overhead that DELETE incurs.

original_questions.question_text: Is DELETE fully transactional (can it be rolled back before commit)?
options: No, DELETE is always immediately permanent
Yes — DELETE participates fully in transactions and can be rolled back before COMMIT
Only if no WHERE clause is used
original_questions.explanation: Unlike DDL on most engines, DELETE (DML) is transactional and reversible before commit.

original_questions.question_text: What is the safety practice recommended before running a DELETE with an uncertain WHERE clause?
options: Run it directly and check the result afterward
Preview the affected rows first with an equivalent SELECT using the same WHERE clause
Always delete without a WHERE clause to be thorough
original_questions.explanation: Previewing with SELECT is the standard, reliable safety practice.

original_questions.question_text: Does DELETE change a table's column structure?
options: No — DELETE only removes rows; columns, indexes, and constraints remain unchanged
DELETE always resets the table's AUTO_INCREMENT counter
original_questions.explanation: DELETE is purely a row-removal operation with no effect on the table's structure.

original_questions.question_text: Can DELETE be filtered to remove only specific rows?
options: No, DELETE always removes every row
Yes — a WHERE clause targets DELETE to only the matching rows
DELETE can only remove exactly one row at a time
original_questions.explanation: WHERE is exactly what makes DELETE selective rather than total.

original_questions.question_text: What trade-off does choosing TRUNCATE over a WHERE-less DELETE involve?
options: No trade-off — TRUNCATE is strictly better in every way
TRUNCATE is typically faster for emptying a whole table, but can't be filtered and, on some engines, offers weaker rollback guarantees
DELETE is always faster than TRUNCATE
TRUNCATE always requires a WHERE clause, unlike DELETE
original_questions.explanation: TRUNCATE's speed advantage comes with reduced flexibility (no filtering) and some transactional caveats.
